title: Core Indicator Words
hook: Clues, not proof. Use these to speed up confirmation of the structure you already see.

blocks.text: Indicator words are structural signals. They are not the argument itself, but they point to where the pieces live. Use them to confirm your structural reading, but never rely on them as a substitute for understanding what is being proved.

blocks.label: The Golden Rule
blocks.body: First find the structure. Then use indicators to speed up confirmation. Always ask: what is being proved, and what is doing the proving?

blocks.text: Core Conclusion Indicators
These usually point to the author’s main claim.

blocks.label: Conclusion indicator
blocks.body: “The library is full every afternoon. **Therefore**, the city should expand library funding.”

blocks.text: Core Premise Indicators (FABS)
FABS is your primary tool for spotting support.

blocks.label: Premise indicator
blocks.body: “The city should expand library funding **because** students rely on the library for tutoring and internet access.”

title: The 2-Part Conclusion Check
hook: The one tool that does not lie. Two questions. Both must be yes.

blocks.text: The check

items: Does the sentence sound like the author’s opinion — a claim that someone could disagree with?
Is the sentence supported by at least one other explicit claim in the stimulus?

blocks.text: Both must be yes. If either is no, the candidate is not the main conclusion. A factual statement fails part one. An unsupported assertion fails part two. A claim the author concedes from someone else fails part one.

blocks.label: Why this works
blocks.body: A conclusion is, by definition, the load-bearing claim of the argument. It is held by the author and supported by something else in the text. Two conditions, no exceptions.

blocks.label: Failure mode
blocks.body: Students often pick the most prominent statistic in the stimulus. A statistic is rarely the conclusion — it is almost always support. Run the 2-Part Check. If you can’t name what supports the statistic, it is not the conclusion.

blocks.text: Apply this on every Main Conclusion question. After enough reps, the check runs in your head before you reach the answer choices.

title: FABS — the support indicator quartet
hook: For. After all. Because. Since. Whatever follows is support — and the conclusion is right next door.

blocks.text: FABS is a memory peg for the four most common premise indicators in LSAT stimuli. Each one introduces a clause that does support work. The conclusion lives next to that clause — usually immediately before, sometimes immediately after.

rows: In the clause before "since" — even when "since" leads the sentence

blocks.label: The since trap
blocks.body: When a stimulus opens with "Since...", the support is up front and the conclusion follows. MC-SIM-Q20 is the canonical example. Train on it.

blocks.label: Read it backwards
blocks.body: Sentence: "We should ban the policy, since it has failed in three pilot programs." → Find FABS ("since") → Support: "it has failed in three pilot programs." → Conclusion: "We should ban the policy."

blocks.text: FABS is decisive in 80% of stimuli. The other 20% need the 2-Part Check (2.B) and Stimulus Tendencies (2.D). Master FABS first.

title: Stimulus Tendencies — where LSAC hides the conclusion
hook: School teaches you the conclusion goes last. The LSAT teaches you it usually does not.

blocks.text: Where the main conclusion actually lives

rows: After a since-clause that opens the stimulus

blocks.label: The number that matters
blocks.body: In more than 90% of Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion is NOT the final claim. The Upside Down Argument pattern is the rule, not the exception.

blocks.text: The two families

items: First-sentence family: author states the claim, rest of the stimulus supports it.
Rebuttal family: author concedes a position, pivots ("but", "however"), states the actual claim, supports it.

blocks.text: The First Sentence vs Rebuttal Lab trains both. The Simulator then sorts every canonical question into one family or the other.

title: The Five Types of Conclusions
hook: Conclusions come in five shapes. Knowing the shape narrows the answer choices.

items: Recommendation — "X should do Y." Often signaled by should, ought, must.
Prediction — "X will Y." Often signaled by will, is going to, is likely to.
Causal claim — "X causes Y." Or X is responsible for Y, X explains Y.
Comparative judgment — "X is better/worse/preferable to Y."
Interpretive claim — "X means/implies/shows that Y." Common in literary or analytical stimuli.

blocks.label: Why type matters
blocks.body: The correct answer matches the type of the author’s claim. A recommendation never resolves to a factual prediction. A causal claim never resolves to a recommendation. Type-mismatch is one of the cleanest tells in the answer choices.

blocks.label: Type-mismatch in distractors
blocks.body: Stimulus argues a recommendation. Answer choice C reads as a prediction ("the policy will succeed"). C is wrong on type alone, before you even check the content.

blocks.text: When two answer choices both restate the conclusion, the one whose grammatical type matches the stimulus wins. Train this in the Conclusion Type Lab.

title: The Rebuttal Structure
hook: Concession → Pivot → Author’s claim → Support. The four-beat skeleton of every rebuttal stimulus.

blocks.text: The four beats

items: Concession — the author grants something. "Granted, X." "It is true that X." "While X is true."
Author’s claim — the actual conclusion. This is the load-bearing sentence.
Support — premises that prop up the claim.

blocks.label: The trick
blocks.body: The concession often sounds like a thesis. It’s a Trojan horse — it sounds bold because the author is briefly inhabiting the opposing view. Wait for the pivot. The conclusion is on the other side.

blocks.label: MC-SIM-Q11 (Letter to the editor)
blocks.body: "I was shocked to learn that Judge Mosston was convicted of criminal assault. Nevertheless, despite his conviction, Mosston should not be forced to resign as judge. He has a long record of community service..."  Concession: "shocked... convicted." Pivot: "Nevertheless." Conclusion: "Mosston should not be forced to resign." Support: community service record.

blocks.text: 11 of the canonical 20 are Rebuttal-family. The First Sentence vs Rebuttal Lab trains the habit of waiting for the pivot before naming the author’s claim.

title: The Three Incorrect-Answer Trap Types (legacy gateway)
source: Notes/Main Conclusion Synopsis.pdf (S) + Notes/Advanced- MP Question Traps_dup1.docx (A)
hook: A starter taxonomy. The full Trap Master expands these to seven traits — but the three patterns underneath every wrong answer live here.

blocks.text: The three patterns

items: Premise as conclusion — the answer lifts a support sentence and floats it as the claim. The most common trap on First-sentence stimuli.
Out of scope — the answer generalizes the claim or imports a topic the stimulus did not address.
Too strong — the answer says something the author would agree with but in a stronger form (more universal, more certain, more specific) than the stimulus warrants.

blocks.label: How this maps to the seven Trap Master traits
blocks.body: T1 absorbs Too strong. T2 absorbs Premise as conclusion. T6 absorbs Out of scope. T3, T4, T5, T7 add finer distinctions. Start with three. Graduate to seven once those click.

blocks.text: On every wrong answer, name the pattern. "Premise-as-conclusion" — done, move on. The naming itself is the diagnostic.

title: Pronoun & Reference Library
hook: Replace the pronoun before you say the conclusion to yourself. Then check the answer choices.

blocks.text: Words to scan for

items: such · this position · this view · these laws · such laws
the policy · the recommendation · the practice (when the antecedent isn’t named in the same sentence)

blocks.label: The Pre-Phrase Goal
blocks.body: When you formulate the conclusion in your own words before checking answers, you must replace every pronoun with the actual reference language from the stimulus. Otherwise the answer choices will look more similar than they are.

blocks.label: Why replacement matters
blocks.body: Conclusion (with pronoun): "This position should not stand." Without replacement, three answer choices look right. With replacement: "The view that Mosston should resign should not stand." Now only one answer matches.

blocks.text: The Main Conclusion Lab trains pronoun replacement on full stimuli. After enough reps it becomes automatic.

title: The Concession Decoder
source: Notes/Argument Core & Periph_dup1.pdf (A) + Notes/Skeletal Breakdown LR (1)_dup1.pdf (A) + Notes/Indicator word list .pdf (A)
hook: Concessions look like agreement. They are setting up the rebuttal.

blocks.text: Concession words

blocks.label: What concessions do
blocks.body: They temporarily inhabit the opposing view. The author is signaling: "I see what you would object with — let me name it briefly so I can refute it." The actual claim follows the pivot.

blocks.text: The structural reveal
Concession → Pivot → Author’s claim → Support. When you see a concession word, the conclusion is not the next sentence. It is the sentence after the pivot.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.body: "Granted, the program has had setbacks. But its long-term outcomes have justified the investment, and continued funding is warranted."  Concession: "setbacks." Pivot: "But." Conclusion: "continued funding is warranted." The "long-term outcomes" sentence is support.

blocks.text: On every Rebuttal-family stimulus, find the concession first. The conclusion is downstream of the pivot. Always.

hook: One page. Print it. Tape it to the desk.

The two families
The seven trap traits

items: T1 — Too strong (specifies a remedy or universal the author did not commit to)
T2 — Premise as conclusion (lifts a support sentence)
T3 — Concession as conclusion (Trojan horse — sounds like the claim, the author is conceding)
T4 — Half the claim (captures part, drops the operative phrase)
T5 — Restated stimulus (paraphrases neutrally without identifying the load-bearing claim)
T6 — Out of scope (generalizes or imports a foreign topic)
T7 — Intermediate conclusion (a sub-claim that supports the main one but is not the main one)

items: State it in your own words. Replace every pronoun with the antecedent.

title: Reference-as-Companion (capstone — implicit)
source: (behavior — RightDrawer overlay handler; not a standalone page)
hook: The Reference is not a destination. It is a companion that pops in beside whatever you are working on.

blocks.text: Open any reference section while inside a lesson, drill, or simulator question and it surfaces in the right drawer in place — no URL change, no scroll loss. Press Esc to dismiss. The companion exists so you never have to leave the work to look something up.

blocks.label: How to invoke
blocks.body: Cmd+K opens the command palette. Type any inventory ID (MC-REF-2.B, NT-FABS, T3) and the matching surface drops into the right drawer. The keyboard cheat sheet in Settings lists every shortcut.

blocks.text: This is not a feature. It is the architectural posture: the curriculum is the surface, the reference is the air, and you should never feel the seam between them.

title: Pivot Indicators
hook: The author is turning. The real claim is on the far side of the pivot.

blocks.text: Pivots mark a transition from one viewpoint (often one the author disagrees with) to the author’s own position.

blocks.label: Conclusion Placement
blocks.body: When a pivot appears, it is a massive signal that the conclusion is arriving. It is almost always in the sentence immediately following the pivot.

title: Opposing View & Concession Indicators
hook: Trojan Horse signals. The author is briefly inhabiting someone else's view.

blocks.text: Opposing View Indicators
Concession Indicators
These are the "Trojan Horse" of the LSAT. They sound like the author’s claim, but they are actually setting up the rebuttal. The author’s conclusion will follow the pivot.

title: Opinion Indicators
hook: Judgments, not facts. Opinions are the most likely conclusion candidates.

blocks.text: A conclusion is, by definition, a claim. Claims are opinions or judgments that require support. Words that signal a judgment often flag the conclusion.

blocks.label: Structure Reading
blocks.body: If you see "should" or "ought," you have a high-probability conclusion candidate. Run the 2-Part Check to confirm it has support.
